q: A 22-year-old male presents with abdominal pain. Which of the following are typical features of acute appendicitis?
options: Initial periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa
Nausea and vomiting after onset of pain
answer: Initial periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa
Nausea and vomiting after onset of pain
explanation: A: Correct. Visceral pain starts periumbilically and migrates to the right iliac fossa once the parietal peritoneum is involved. B: Incorrect. Pain is not relieved by defecation, so this is not a feature of appendicitis. C: Correct. Anorexia is one of the earliest and most consistent symptoms. D: Correct. Vomiting typically follows the onset of pain. E: Incorrect. Early appendicitis causes low-grade fever. High-grade fever suggests perforation or another complication.

q: Which signs are associated with acute appendicitis?
explanation: A: Correct. McBurney's point tenderness marks the point of maximal tenderness over the appendix. B: Correct. Left-sided palpation causes right iliac fossa pain through transmitted pressure in the colon. C: Incorrect. Murphy's sign is a sign of acute cholecystitis, not appendicitis. D: Correct. Pain on extending the hip indicates an inflamed retrocaecal appendix touching the psoas muscle. E: Correct. Pain on internal rotation of the hip indicates a pelvic appendix touching the obturator internus.

q: Which findings support a diagnosis of appendicitis?
options: Normal white blood cell count excludes appendicitis
CT scan showing appendiceal wall thickening
answer: CT scan showing appendiceal wall thickening
explanation: A: Correct. Neutrophilic leucocytosis supports an inflammatory or infective process. B: Correct. CRP is a non-specific acute-phase reactant that rises in appendicitis. C: Incorrect. A normal white cell count does not exclude appendicitis. D: Correct. A non-compressible, blind-ending tubular structure on ultrasound is the key diagnostic sign. E: Correct. CT showing a thickened appendiceal wall (over about 6 mm) supports the diagnosis.

q: Which of the following are complications of untreated appendicitis?
explanation: A: Correct. Untreated inflammation can progress to perforation. B: Correct. Perforation leads to generalised peritonitis. C: Correct. Localised perforation can form an appendicular abscess. D: Correct. Adhesions or the inflammatory mass can cause intestinal obstruction, though this is less common. E: Incorrect. Chronic pancreatitis is not a complication of appendicitis.

q: Which are appropriate management options for appendicitis?
explanation: A: Correct. Emergency appendicectomy is the standard treatment. B: Correct. IV antibiotics are given as part of management. C: Correct. Selected uncomplicated cases can be managed with antibiotics, with appendicectomy considered later. D: Incorrect. Discharge without follow-up is unsafe. E: Correct. Abscesses are drained, usually percutaneously, with interval surgery considered.

q: Which of the following are common features of hyperthyroidism?
explanation: A: Correct. Hypermetabolism causes weight loss despite increased appetite. B: Correct. Excess thyroid hormone increases heat production, causing heat intolerance. C: Incorrect. Hyperthyroidism causes tachycardia, not bradycardia. D: Correct. Increased adrenergic activity causes fine tremor. E: Incorrect. Hyperthyroidism more often causes diarrhoea and more frequent bowel movements than constipation.

q: Which of the following are features of hypothyroidism?
explanation: A: Correct. Reduced metabolic rate causes weight gain. B: Correct. Reduced heat production causes cold intolerance. C: Incorrect. Hypothyroidism causes hyporeflexia with delayed relaxation, not hyperreflexia. D: Correct. Reduced cardiac output and rate cause bradycardia. E: Correct. Reduced sweating and altered skin metabolism cause dry skin.

q: Which conditions can cause hyperthyroidism?
explanation: A: Correct. Graves' disease is the most common cause. B: Correct. Toxic multinodular goitre causes autonomous hormone production. C: Correct. Hashimoto thyroiditis can produce a transient thyrotoxic phase (hashitoxicosis) as follicles are damaged. D: Correct. Subacute thyroiditis causes a painful, transient thyrotoxic phase. E: Incorrect. Iodine deficiency causes goitre and hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism.

q: Which are complications of untreated thyroid disorders?
explanation: A: Correct. Thyroid storm is a life-threatening complication of thyrotoxicosis. B: Correct. Myxoedema coma is the severe complication of untreated hypothyroidism. C: Correct. Thyroid hormone excess can cause atrial fibrillation. D: Correct. Thyroid hormone excess increases bone turnover and causes osteoporosis. E: Incorrect. Acute pancreatitis is not a recognised complication of thyroid disease.

q: Which of the following are appropriate in evaluating or managing thyroid disease?
explanation: A: Correct. TSH is the first-line screening test. B: Correct. Free T4 confirms the biochemical state. C: Correct. Radioactive iodine uptake helps differentiate Graves' disease and toxic goitre from thyroiditis. D: Correct. Beta-blockers control symptoms of thyrotoxicosis while definitive treatment takes effect. E: Incorrect. Antibiotics have no role in routine thyroid disease management.

q: Which of the following are clinical features of hyperparathyroidism?
explanation: A: Correct. Bone resorption causes bone pain. B: Correct. Hypercalciuria leads to calcium phosphate renal stones. C: Correct. Hypercalcaemia reduces gut motility and causes constipation. D: Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia causes hyporeflexia, not hyperreflexia. E: Correct. Depression is a recognised neuropsychiatric feature ("psychic moans").

q: Which of the following are features of hypoparathyroidism?
explanation: A: Correct. Hypocalcaemia causes tetany. B: Correct. Chvostek's sign is facial nerve twitching when tapped, a sign of neuromuscular irritability. C: Correct. Trousseau's sign is carpopedal spasm after cuff inflation, also a sign of hypocalcaemia. D: Incorrect. Hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcaemia, not hypercalcaemia. E: Correct. Severe hypocalcaemia causes seizures.

q: Which conditions can cause hyperparathyroidism?
explanation: A: Correct. A parathyroid adenoma is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism. B: Correct. CKD causes secondary hyperparathyroidism through phosphate retention and reduced vitamin D activation. C: Correct. Vitamin D deficiency causes secondary hyperparathyroidism through low calcium absorption. D: Correct. Parathyroid carcinoma is a rare cause of primary hyperparathyroidism. E: Incorrect. Hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion and action, so it causes hypoparathyroidism.

q: Which are complications of prolonged hyperparathyroidism?
explanation: A: Correct. Osteoporosis results from chronic bone resorption. B: Correct. Weakened bone leads to pathological fractures. C: Correct. Hypercalciuria and calcium deposition cause nephrocalcinosis. D: Correct. Hypercalcaemia increases gastrin secretion and gastric acid, causing peptic ulcer disease. E: Incorrect. Hypotension is not a recognised complication of prolonged hyperparathyroidism.

q: Which of the following are appropriate in evaluating or managing parathyroid disease?
explanation: A: Correct. Serum calcium is the first-line test. B: Correct. PTH level distinguishes primary from secondary hyperparathyroidism. C: Correct. Phosphate is low in primary hyperparathyroidism and high in CKD, helping to classify the disorder. D: Correct. Neck ultrasound or sestamibi scanning localises the parathyroid adenoma. E: Incorrect. Antibiotics have no role in routine parathyroid disease management.

q: Which of the following are actions of calcitonin?
options: Secreted by parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid
answer: Secreted by parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid
explanation: A: Correct. Calcitonin lowers serum calcium. B: Correct. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclast activity, reducing bone resorption. C: Correct. Calcitonin increases renal calcium excretion. D: Incorrect. Calcitonin reduces, not increases, intestinal calcium absorption. E: Correct. Calcitonin is secreted by the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid.

q: Which of the following are features of medullary thyroid carcinoma?
explanation: A: Correct. Calcitonin is the tumour marker and is raised in MTC. B: Correct. MTC arises from the parafollicular C cells. C: Correct. Familial MTC occurs in MEN 2A and MEN 2B. D: Incorrect. MTC does not cause hypocalcaemia; calcitonin lowers calcium only mildly. E: Correct. Calcitonin and other peptides secreted by the tumour cause secretory diarrhoea.

q: Which of the following are associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma in MEN syndromes?
explanation: A: Correct. Phaeochromocytoma occurs in MEN 2A and MEN 2B. B: Correct. Primary hyperparathyroidism occurs in MEN 2A. C: Incorrect. Pituitary adenoma is a feature of MEN 1, not MEN 2. D: Correct. Mucosal neuromas are a feature of MEN 2B. E: Correct. Marfanoid habitus is a feature of MEN 2B.

q: Which of the following are useful in diagnosing or monitoring calcitonin-related disease?
explanation: A: Correct. Serum calcitonin is the diagnostic and monitoring marker for MTC. B: Correct. CEA is used alongside calcitonin for monitoring MTC. C: Incorrect. Thyroid function tests do not diagnose or monitor MTC; they assess thyroid function generally. D: Correct. RET testing identifies hereditary MTC and guides screening of relatives. E: Incorrect. Serum amylase has no role in MTC.

q: Which of the following are appropriate management strategies for medullary thyroid carcinoma?
options: Prophylactic thyroidectomy in RET mutation carriers
answer: Prophylactic thyroidectomy in RET mutation carriers
explanation: A: Correct. Total thyroidectomy is the standard treatment for MTC. B: Correct. Prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended for RET mutation carriers, timed by the mutation's risk level. C: Incorrect. MTC does not take up radioactive iodine, so RAI is ineffective. D: Correct. Postoperative calcitonin monitoring detects residual or recurrent disease. E: Incorrect. Chemotherapy is not first-line; MTC is generally managed surgically first.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain how calcitonin lowers serum calcium?
explanation: A: Correct. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclasts. B: Correct. Reduced osteoclast activity decreases bone resorption and calcium release. C: Correct. Calcitonin increases renal calcium excretion. D: Incorrect. Calcitonin does not increase intestinal calcium absorption; if anything it reduces it. E: Correct. Calcitonin acts as a physiological antagonist to PTH.

q: Which of the following explain the pathophysiology of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC)?
explanation: A: Correct. MTC arises from parafollicular C cells. B: Correct. The tumour cells produce excess calcitonin. C: Correct. Activating RET mutations drive the tumour's development. D: Incorrect. MTC is not a cause of excess thyroxine; the tumour secretes calcitonin, not T4. E: Correct. MTC is a neuroendocrine tumour, which explains its peptide secretion.

q: Which mechanisms contribute to diarrhea in medullary thyroid carcinoma?
explanation: A: Correct. Tumour-secreted VIP causes secretory diarrhoea. B: Correct, though a weaker mechanism. Peptide hormones increase intestinal motility, which adds to diarrhoea alongside secretion. C: Incorrect. Calcitonin's calcium-lowering effect does not cause diarrhoea. D: Correct. Neuroendocrine peptide secretion causes the diarrhoea. E: Incorrect. Pancreatic insufficiency is not a feature of MTC.

q: Which of the following reflect the underlying pathophysiology of MEN 2 syndromes?
options: RET gene mutation causing uncontrolled cell growth
answer: RET gene mutation causing uncontrolled cell growth
explanation: A: Correct. Activating RET mutations cause uncontrolled cell growth. B: Correct. The mutation produces multiple endocrine neoplasms. C: Correct. The affected tissues are derived from neural crest cells. D: Incorrect. MEN 2 is a neoplastic disorder, not an autoimmune one. E: Correct. MEN 2 is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Inheritance is not strictly a mechanism, but it is a correct fact about the syndrome.

q: Which explain why radioactive iodine is ineffective in medullary thyroid carcinoma?
options: C cells do not uptake iodine
Tumor is not derived from follicular cells
Tumor cells are resistant due to high calcium levels
answer: C cells do not uptake iodine
Tumor is not derived from follicular cells
explanation: A: Correct. C cells do not take up iodine. B: Correct. MTC arises from neural crest-derived C cells, not follicular cells. C: Correct. C cells do not produce thyroglobulin, so iodine is not incorporated. D: Correct. C cells lack the sodium-iodide symporter. E: Incorrect. High calcium does not make tumour cells resistant to radioiodine.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain how calcitonin regulates calcium homeostasis?
options: Decreases release of calcium from bone
Acts as a physiological antagonist to parathyroid hormone (PTH)
answer: Decreases release of calcium from bone
Acts as a physiological antagonist to parathyroid hormone (PTH)
explanation: A: Correct. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. B: Correct. Calcitonin reduces calcium release from bone. C: Correct. Calcitonin increases renal calcium excretion. D: Incorrect. Calcitonin reduces intestinal calcium absorption rather than increasing it. E: Correct. Calcitonin opposes the calcium-raising effects of PTH.

q: Which of the following describe the underlying pathophysiology of medullary thyroid carcinoma?
explanation: A: Correct. The tumour originates from parafollicular C cells. B: Correct. The tumour excessively produces calcitonin. C: Correct. RET proto-oncogene mutation drives tumour formation. D: Incorrect. MTC does not produce thyroid hormone; it secretes calcitonin. E: Correct. MTC is a neuroendocrine tumour.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain diarrhea seen in medullary thyroid carcinoma?
options: Increased gut motility due to peptide hormones
Direct effect of calcitonin on intestinal mucosa
Neuroendocrine tumor secretion of bioactive substances
answer: Increased gut motility due to peptide hormones
Neuroendocrine tumor secretion of bioactive substances
explanation: A: Correct. VIP secreted by the tumour causes secretory diarrhoea. B: Correct. Tumour-driven peptides increase intestinal secretion. C: Correct. Peptide hormones increase gut motility, adding to diarrhoea. D: Incorrect. There is no established direct effect of calcitonin on intestinal mucosa causing diarrhoea. The key includes this, and I disagree. E: Correct. The neuroendocrine tumour secretes several bioactive substances that cause diarrhoea.

q: Which of the following reflect the pathophysiological basis of MEN 2 syndromes?
explanation: A: Correct. An activating RET mutation is the underlying molecular defect. B: Correct. Multiple endocrine neoplasms develop. C: Correct. Neural crest-derived tissues are affected. D: Incorrect. Autoimmune destruction is not the mechanism of MEN 2. E: Correct. MEN 2 is autosomal dominant.

q: Which of the following explain why radioactive iodine is ineffective in medullary thyroid carcinoma?
options: Parafollicular C cells do not uptake iodine
Absence of sodium-iodide symporters in tumor cells
Resistance due to elevated calcitonin levels
answer: Parafollicular C cells do not uptake iodine
Absence of sodium-iodide symporters in tumor cells
explanation: A: Correct. MTC arises from non-follicular cells. B: Correct. Parafollicular C cells do not take up iodine. C: Correct. Tumour cells lack the sodium-iodide symporter. D: Correct. C cells do not produce thyroglobulin. E: Incorrect. Elevated calcitonin does not make tumours resistant to radioiodine; the cause is the absence of iodine uptake.

q: Which of the following explain the typical progression of pain in acute appendicitis?
options: Initial visceral pain due to midgut innervation
Referred pain to the periumbilical region
Later somatic pain localized to the right iliac fossa
Pain caused primarily by gastric irritation
Involvement of parietal peritoneum leading to localized tenderness
answer: Initial visceral pain due to midgut innervation
Referred pain to the periumbilical region
Later somatic pain localized to the right iliac fossa
Involvement of parietal peritoneum leading to localized tenderness
explanation: A: Correct. Early pain is visceral, from midgut innervation. B: Correct. Visceral pain is referred to the periumbilical region. C: Correct. Later somatic pain localises to the right iliac fossa. D: Incorrect. Appendicitis pain is not caused primarily by gastric irritation. E: Correct. Parietal peritoneal involvement causes localised tenderness.

q: Which of the following contribute to the pathophysiology of acute appendicitis?
explanation: A: Correct. Luminal obstruction by a faecolith starts the process. B: Correct. Raised intraluminal pressure impairs blood flow. C: Correct. Venous congestion leads to ischaemia. D: Correct. Bacterial overgrowth drives the infection. E: Incorrect. Perforation follows prolonged inflammation, not occurring without it.

q: Which of the following signs can be explained by the anatomical position and inflammatory process of the appendix?
options: Rovsing’s sign due to peritoneal irritation
Murphy’s sign due to appendiceal inflammation
Rebound tenderness due to peritoneal inflammation
answer: Rovsing’s sign due to peritoneal irritation
Rebound tenderness due to peritoneal inflammation
explanation: A: Correct. Rovsing's sign reflects peritoneal irritation from pressure transmitted through the colon. B: Correct. A retrocaecal appendix contacts the psoas, causing the psoas sign. C: Correct. A pelvic appendix contacts the obturator internus, causing the obturator sign. D: Incorrect. Murphy's sign is a gallbladder sign, not an appendiceal one. E: Correct. Rebound tenderness reflects peritoneal inflammation.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain complications of untreated appendicitis?
options: Spread of infection to peritoneal cavity
answer: Spread of infection to peritoneal cavity
explanation: A: Correct. Ischaemic necrosis of the wall leads to perforation. B: Correct. Increased intraluminal pressure can cause perforation. C: Correct. Infection spreads into the peritoneal cavity after perforation. D: Correct. Localised abscesses form when spread is contained. E: Incorrect. Appendicitis does not progress directly to chronic pancreatitis.

q: Which of the following are explained by the inflammatory and infectious process in appendicitis?
options: Elevated CRP as an acute-phase reactant
answer: Elevated CRP as an acute-phase reactant
explanation: A: Correct. Inflammation causes neutrophilic leucocytosis. B: Correct. Cytokines released during inflammation cause fever. C: Correct. Visceral inflammation suppresses appetite, causing anorexia. D: Incorrect. Vomiting follows pain in appendicitis, not precedes it. E: Correct. CRP is an acute-phase reactant raised by inflammation.

q: Which of the following explain the pathophysiology of hyperthyroidism?
explanation: A: Correct. Thyroid hormone increases basal metabolic rate. B: Correct. Thyroid hormone upregulates beta-adrenergic receptors, increasing sensitivity to catecholamines. C: Correct. Increased metabolic activity raises heat production. D: Incorrect. Oxygen consumption increases in hyperthyroidism, not decreases. E: Correct. Enhanced sympathetic activity contributes to tachycardia and tremor.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain features of hypothyroidism?
explanation: A: Correct. Reduced metabolic activity is the basis of hypothyroid symptoms. B: Correct. Glycosaminoglycan accumulation causes the non-pitting oedema of myxoedema. C: Correct. Reduced sympathetic activity contributes to bradycardia and fatigue. D: Incorrect. Thermogenesis is reduced in hypothyroidism. E: Correct. Reduced cardiac function causes bradycardia and slow contractility.

q: Which of the following describe the pathophysiology of Graves’ disease?
options: Increased synthesis of T3 and T4
answer: Increased synthesis of T3 and T4
explanation: A: Correct. TSH receptor-stimulating autoantibodies drive hormone production. B: Correct. Autoantibody stimulation increases T3 and T4 synthesis. C: Correct. Diffuse thyroid enlargement occurs. D: Incorrect. Graves' disease stimulates follicles rather than destroying them. E: Correct. Orbital fibroblast activity causes the ophthalmopathy.

q: Which of the following explain the life-threatening features of thyroid storm?
options: Hypermetabolic state leading to organ dysfunction
Increased heat production leading to hyperpyrexia
answer: Hypermetabolic state leading to organ dysfunction
Increased heat production leading to hyperpyrexia
explanation: A: Correct. Tissues respond exaggeratedly to thyroid hormone. B: Correct. Catecholamine sensitivity increases massively. C: Correct. The hypermetabolic state causes organ dysfunction. D: Incorrect. Thyroid storm is a hyperthyroid crisis, not a hypothyroid state. E: Correct. Increased heat production causes hyperpyrexia.

q: Which of the following explain the mechanism of Hashimoto thyroiditis?
options: Lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland
answer: Lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland
explanation: A: Correct. Autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue occurs. B: Correct. Anti-TPO antibodies are characteristic. C: Correct. Lymphocytic infiltration is the histological hallmark. D: Incorrect. Hashimoto thyroiditis reduces, rather than increases, hormone production over time. E: Correct. Progressive fibrosis follows chronic inflammation.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain hypercalcemia in hyperparathyroidism?
options: Increased intestinal calcium absorption via vitamin D activation
answer: Increased intestinal calcium absorption via vitamin D activation
explanation: A: Correct. PTH stimulates osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. B: Correct. PTH increases renal calcium reabsorption. C: Correct. PTH activates vitamin D, increasing intestinal calcium absorption. D: Incorrect. PTH increases renal phosphate excretion, so phosphate excretion is not decreased. E: Correct. PTH increases activation of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.

q: Which of the following explain hypocalcemia in hypoparathyroidism?
options: Increased calcium absorption from the gut
explanation: A: Correct. Without PTH, osteoclast activity falls. B: Correct. Renal calcium reabsorption falls without PTH. C: Correct. Reduced PTH lowers 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D activation. D: Correct. Phosphate retention follows from loss of PTH's phosphaturic effect. E: Incorrect. Calcium absorption from the gut falls when vitamin D activation falls.

q: Which of the following contribute to bone changes in hyperparathyroidism?
options: Replacement of bone with fibrous tissue
answer: Replacement of bone with fibrous tissue
explanation: A: Correct. Osteoclastic resorption is increased. B: Correct. Bone is replaced by fibrous tissue, causing osteitis fibrosa cystica. C: Correct. Brown tumours are focal fibrous and haemorrhagic lesions of bone. D: Incorrect. Bone mineral density falls in hyperparathyroidism. E: Correct. Subperiosteal resorption is characteristic, especially in the phalanges.

q: Which of the following explain neuromuscular irritability in hypocalcemia?
options: Lower threshold for action potential generation
Reduced calcium stabilization of nerve membranes
answer: Lower threshold for action potential generation
Reduced calcium stabilization of nerve membranes
explanation: A: Correct. Hypocalcaemia increases neuronal excitability. B: Correct. The action potential threshold falls. C: Correct. Sodium permeability increases when calcium no longer stabilises the membrane. D: Correct. Calcium normally stabilises nerve membranes, so reduced calcium destabilises them. E: Incorrect. Reflex activity is increased in hypocalcaemia, not decreased.

q: Which of the following explain the pathophysiology of secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease?
options: Direct suppression of PTH by kidneys
explanation: A: Correct. Reduced phosphate excretion causes hyperphosphataemia, which lowers calcium and stimulates PTH. B: Correct. The kidney's failure to activate vitamin D reduces calcium absorption. C: Correct. Hypocalcaemia directly stimulates PTH secretion. D: Incorrect. The kidneys do not directly suppress PTH; their failure drives secondary hyperparathyroidism. E: Correct. Chronic stimulation causes parathyroid hyperplasia.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain the development of peritonitis?
options: Bacterial contamination of the peritoneal cavity
answer: Bacterial contamination of the peritoneal cavity
explanation: A: Correct. Bacterial contamination is the commonest cause. B: Correct. Chemical irritants such as gastric acid or bile inflame the peritoneum. C: Correct. Inflammatory cytokines drive the response. D: Incorrect. The peritoneum is affected in peritonitis, so it is not sterile and unaffected. E: Correct. Vascular permeability increases, allowing fluid and cells to leak.

q: Which of the following explain the severe abdominal pain in peritonitis?
options: Guarding due to reflex muscle contraction
answer: Guarding due to reflex muscle contraction
explanation: A: Correct. Irritation of the parietal peritoneum causes severe pain. B: Correct. Somatic nerves in the parietal peritoneum carry the pain. C: Correct. Parietal pain is sharp and well localised. D: Incorrect. Visceral pain alone is typically vague and poorly localised, not the severe pain of peritonitis. E: Correct. Guarding is a reflex muscle contraction that protects inflamed peritoneum.

q: Which of the following explain systemic manifestations of peritonitis?
options: Increased cardiac output in late stage shock
explanation: A: Correct. Fluid sequesters into the inflamed peritoneal cavity. B: Correct. Fluid loss causes hypovolaemia. C: Correct. Bacterial translocation causes sepsis. D: Incorrect. Cardiac output falls in late shock, rather than rising. E: Correct. Inflammatory mediators drive systemic illness.

q: Which of the following are causes or types of peritonitis?
explanation: A: Correct. Perforated appendicitis causes secondary peritonitis. B: Correct. Perforated peptic ulcer causes peritonitis. C: Correct. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is a primary peritonitis, typically in ascites. D: Correct. Acute pancreatitis can cause chemical peritonitis. E: Incorrect. Myocardial infarction does not cause peritonitis.

q: Which of the following explain the clinical signs seen in peritonitis?
options: Rebound tenderness due to peritoneal irritation
Reduced bowel sounds due to ileus
answer: Rebound tenderness due to peritoneal irritation
Reduced bowel sounds due to ileus
explanation: A: Correct. Rebound tenderness reflects peritoneal irritation. B: Correct. Board-like rigidity is caused by reflex muscle spasm over the inflamed peritoneum. C: Correct. Ileus from peritonitis reduces bowel sounds. D: Incorrect. Hyperactive bowel sounds suggest mechanical obstruction, not peritonitis. E: Correct. Fever reflects the inflammatory response.

q: Which of the following mechanisms contribute to the development of acute cholecystitis?
options: Obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones
Increased intraluminal pressure in the gallbladder
answer: Obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones
Increased intraluminal pressure in the gallbladder
explanation: A: Correct. Cystic duct obstruction by a gallstone is the primary cause. B: Correct. Raised pressure in the gallbladder damages the wall. C: Correct. Ischaemia of the wall follows raised pressure. D: Correct. Stasis leads to secondary bacterial infection. E: Incorrect. Perforation follows inflammation, not occurs without it.

q: Which of the following explain the characteristic pain in cholecystitis?
options: Visceral pain referred to the epigastrium or right upper quadrant
Irritation of the parietal peritoneum causing localized tenderness
Referred pain to the right shoulder or scapula
Pain relieved by eating fatty meals
answer: Visceral pain referred to the epigastrium or right upper quadrant
Irritation of the parietal peritoneum causing localized tenderness
Referred pain to the right shoulder or scapula
explanation: A: Correct. Gallbladder distension causes visceral pain. B: Correct. Visceral pain is referred to the epigastrium and right upper quadrant. C: Correct. Peritoneal irritation later causes localised tenderness. D: Correct. Diaphragmatic irritation refers pain to the right shoulder or scapula. E: Incorrect. Cholecystitis pain is typically worsened by fatty meals, not relieved by them.

q: Which of the following explain the mechanism of Murphy’s sign?
options: Inflamed gallbladder contacts examiner’s hand during inspiration
answer: Inflamed gallbladder contacts examiner’s hand during inspiration
explanation: A: Correct. The inflamed gallbladder contacts the examiner's hand on inspiration, causing pain. B: Correct. The descending diaphragm pushes the gallbladder onto the examiner's hand. C: Correct. Sudden pain causes the patient to stop inspiration. D: Incorrect. The sign is not due to inflammation of the hepatic capsule. E: Correct. The sign reflects localised peritoneal irritation of the gallbladder.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain complications of untreated cholecystitis?
options: Gallbladder wall necrosis due to ischemia
Direct progression to pancreatitis without obstruction
answer: Gallbladder wall necrosis due to ischemia
explanation: A: Correct. Ischaemia causes gallbladder wall necrosis. B: Correct. Perforation leads to peritonitis. C: Correct. Empyema forms when the gallbladder fills with pus. D: Correct. Fistulae can form with adjacent organs such as the duodenum or colon. E: Incorrect. Pancreatitis from a cholecystitis usually follows duct obstruction, not occurs without it.

q: Which of the following are explained by the inflammatory process in cholecystitis?
explanation: A: Correct. Leucocytosis reflects the inflammatory response. B: Correct. CRP rises in acute inflammation. C: Correct. Cytokines release causes fever. D: Incorrect. Bilirubin is not raised in all cases; it is raised only if the common bile duct is obstructed. E: Correct. Mild elevation of liver enzymes is common from inflammation or transient obstruction.

q: Which of the following mechanisms contribute to the formation of gallstones?
explanation: A: Correct. Supersaturated bile with cholesterol is the basis of cholesterol stones. B: Correct. Gallbladder stasis allows crystals to form. C: Incorrect. Bile salt concentration is reduced, not increased, in gallstone formation. D: Correct. Nucleation of cholesterol crystals begins stone formation. E: Correct. Mucus hypersecretion traps crystals within the gallbladder.

q: Which of the following correctly describe the pathophysiology of different gallstones?
options: Cholesterol stones are due to supersaturation of cholesterol
Pigment stones are associated with hemolysis
Black pigment stones are linked to sterile bile
Brown pigment stones are associated with infection
Cholesterol stones are primarily composed of bilirubin
answer: Cholesterol stones are due to supersaturation of cholesterol
Pigment stones are associated with hemolysis
Black pigment stones are linked to sterile bile
Brown pigment stones are associated with infection
explanation: A: Correct. Cholesterol stones form from supersaturated cholesterol bile. B: Correct. Pigment stones are associated with haemolysis, which raises bilirubin. C: Correct. Black pigment stones form in sterile bile, typically in haemolysis or cirrhosis. D: Correct. Brown pigment stones are associated with biliary infection. E: Incorrect. Cholesterol stones are composed mainly of cholesterol, not bilirubin.

q: Which of the following explain the pain in biliary colic?
options: Transient obstruction of the cystic duct
Ischemia of the gallbladder wall (early stage)
answer: Transient obstruction of the cystic duct
explanation: A: Correct. Intermittent obstruction of the cystic duct causes colic. B: Correct. The gallbladder contracts against the obstruction, causing pain. C: Correct. Raised intraluminal pressure causes the pain. D: Incorrect. Ischaemia of the wall is a feature of acute cholecystitis, not early biliary colic. E: Correct. Fatty meals trigger gallbladder contraction through cholecystokinin.

q: Which of the following factors increase the risk of gallstone formation?
explanation: A: Correct. Female sex is a risk factor. B: Correct. Obesity increases cholesterol saturation of bile. C: Correct. Rapid weight loss increases cholesterol supersaturation. D: Correct. Pregnancy increases cholesterol saturation and gallbladder stasis. E: Incorrect. A high bile salt concentration is protective, not a risk factor.

q: Which of the following complications can arise from cholelithiasis based on pathophysiology?
explanation: A: Correct. Cystic duct obstruction causes acute cholecystitis. B: Correct. Common bile duct stones cause choledocholithiasis. C: Correct. Ampullary obstruction causes acute pancreatitis. D: Correct. Gallstone ileus results from a stone passing through a cholecystoduodenal fistula. E: Incorrect. Primary hyperparathyroidism is not caused by gallstones.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain choledocholithiasis?
options: Migration of gallstones from the gallbladder into the common bile duct
Primary stone formation within the bile duct
Increased bile drainage into the duodenum
answer: Migration of gallstones from the gallbladder into the common bile duct
Primary stone formation within the bile duct
explanation: A: Correct. Gallstones migrate from the gallbladder into the common bile duct. B: Correct. Stones can also form primarily within the bile duct. C: Correct. The stone obstructs bile flow. D: Incorrect. Bile drainage into the duodenum is reduced, not increased, by the obstruction. E: Correct. Biliary stasis promotes bacterial infection, leading to cholangitis.

q: Which of the following explain jaundice in choledocholithiasis?
options: Obstruction of bile flow from liver to intestine
Accumulation of conjugated bilirubin in blood
Increased excretion of bilirubin into stool
Dark urine due to water-soluble bilirubin
Pale stools due to lack of bile pigments
answer: Obstruction of bile flow from liver to intestine
Accumulation of conjugated bilirubin in blood
Dark urine due to water-soluble bilirubin
Pale stools due to lack of bile pigments
explanation: A: Correct. Bile flow from the liver to the intestine is obstructed. B: Correct. Conjugated bilirubin regurgitates into the blood. C: Incorrect. Bilirubin excretion into stool falls, which is why stools become pale. D: Correct. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble, so it is excreted in urine, making it dark. E: Correct. Without bile pigment in the gut, stools become pale.

q: Which of the following mechanisms contribute to ascending cholangitis?
explanation: A: Correct. Biliary obstruction is the key initiating event. B: Correct. Bacteria ascend from the duodenum into the bile duct. C: Correct. Raised intrabiliary pressure drives bacteria into the circulation. D: Incorrect. Bile is not sterile in cholangitis; it becomes infected. E: Correct. Infection can spread systemically, causing septicaemia.

q: Which of the following are explained by bile duct obstruction?
explanation: A: Correct. Biliary obstruction causes right upper quadrant pain. B: Correct. Obstruction causes jaundice. C: Correct. Cholangitis causes fever. D: Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia is not a feature of bile duct obstruction. E: Correct. Retained bile salts in the blood cause pruritus.

q: Which of the following complications are explained by the pathophysiology of bile duct obstruction?
explanation: A: Correct. Acute cholangitis is an infection of obstructed bile. B: Correct. Obstruction of the ampulla causes acute pancreatitis. C: Correct. Prolonged obstruction leads to secondary biliary cirrhosis. D: Correct. Infection of the obstructed bile can spread to form liver abscesses. E: Incorrect. Acute appendicitis is not caused by bile duct obstruction.

q: Which of the following mechanisms contribute to the development of acute pancreatitis?
options: Premature activation of pancreatic enzymes within the pancreas
Activation of trypsinogen to trypsin inside acinar cells
Increased insulin secretion as the primary event
answer: Premature activation of pancreatic enzymes within the pancreas
Activation of trypsinogen to trypsin inside acinar cells
explanation: A: Correct. Premature enzyme activation inside the pancreas causes autodigestion. B: Correct. Autodigestion of pancreatic tissue is the central mechanism. C: Correct. Duct obstruction by gallstones causes pancreatitis. D: Correct. Trypsinogen is activated to trypsin inside acinar cells, starting the cascade. E: Incorrect. Increased insulin secretion is not a mechanism of acute pancreatitis.

q: Which of the following explain systemic complications of acute pancreatitis?
explanation: A: Correct. Cytokines drive the systemic inflammatory response. B: Correct. Vascular permeability increases, leading to fluid leak. C: Correct. Third spacing of fluid into the retroperitoneum and peritoneum occurs. D: Correct. Fluid loss and vasodilation cause hypovolaemia and shock. E: Incorrect. The inflammatory response is increased in pancreatitis, not decreased.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain complications of pancreatitis?
options: Fat necrosis due to lipase activity
answer: Fat necrosis due to lipase activity
explanation: A: Correct. Released lipase causes fat necrosis. B: Correct. Fluid collections become pseudocysts. C: Correct. Erosion of vessels causes haemorrhage. D: Correct. Systemic inflammation can cause ARDS. E: Incorrect. Fibrosis develops in chronic pancreatitis, not in early disease.

q: Which of the following are explained by the underlying pathophysiology of pancreatitis?
options: Hyperglycemia due to islet cell injury
answer: Hyperglycemia due to islet cell injury
explanation: A: Correct. Pancreatic injury releases amylase and lipase into the blood. B: Correct. Calcium binds to fatty acids in fat necrosis (saponification), causing hypocalcaemia. C: Correct. Islet cell injury causes hyperglycaemia. D: Incorrect. Bowel sounds are reduced in pancreatitis due to ileus. E: Correct. Fever reflects the inflammatory response.

q: Which of the following structures are closely related to the head of the pancreas?
explanation: A: Correct. The C-shaped duodenum wraps around the pancreatic head. B: Correct. The common bile duct runs through the posterior head. C: Correct. The IVC lies posterior to the pancreatic head. D: Incorrect. The spleen lies in the left upper quadrant, away from the head. E: Correct. The superior mesenteric vessels run close to the head and neck.

q: Which of the following explain obstructive jaundice caused by a lesion in the head of the pancreas?
options: Compression of the common bile duct
Impaired bile flow into the duodenum
Accumulation of conjugated bilirubin in blood
answer: Compression of the common bile duct
Impaired bile flow into the duodenum
Accumulation of conjugated bilirubin in blood
explanation: A: Correct. A pancreatic head lesion compresses the common bile duct. B: Correct. Bile flow into the duodenum is impaired. C: Correct. Conjugated bilirubin accumulates in the blood. D: Incorrect. Bile secretion does not increase; the obstruction blocks its flow. E: Correct. Pale stools and dark urine result from the obstruction.

q: Which of the following are typical features of carcinoma of the head of the pancreas?
explanation: A: Correct. Jaundice is typically painless and progressive. B: Correct. Courvoisier's sign is a palpable, non-tender gallbladder from biliary obstruction. C: Correct. Weight loss is a common feature. D: Incorrect. Pain is typically a late feature, not severe and early. E: Correct. Pruritus results from retained bile salts.

q: Which of the following mechanisms occur when the pancreatic duct is obstructed at the head?
explanation: A: Correct. Enzymes cannot drain from the pancreas. B: Correct. Intraductal pressure rises behind the obstruction. C: Correct. Raised pressure causes inflammation. D: Correct. Reduced enzyme delivery to the duodenum impairs fat digestion. E: Incorrect. Insulin secretion is not increased by pancreatic duct obstruction.

q: Which of the following complications can arise due to pathology at the head of the pancreas?
explanation: A: Correct. Obstructive jaundice results from compression of the bile duct. B: Correct. Biliary obstruction predisposes to ascending cholangitis. C: Correct. Duct obstruction causes acute pancreatitis. D: Correct. A large head lesion can compress the duodenum, causing gastric outlet obstruction. E: Incorrect. Splenic rupture is not caused by pancreatic head pathology.

q: Which of the following explain the development of annular pancreas?
options: Failure of normal rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud
Persistence of a bifid ventral bud encircling the duodenum
Abnormal fusion of dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds
Complete absence of the dorsal pancreatic bud
Encirclement of the second part of the duodenum
answer: Failure of normal rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud
Persistence of a bifid ventral bud encircling the duodenum
Encirclement of the second part of the duodenum
explanation: A: Correct. Failure of normal ventral bud rotation allows the bud to encircle the duodenum. B: Correct. A bifid ventral bud persists and encircles the duodenum. C: Incorrect. Dorsal and ventral bud fusion is normal, and abnormal fusion is not the recognised cause. The key includes this, and I disagree. D: Incorrect. The dorsal bud is not absent in annular pancreas; the problem is the ventral bud. E: Correct. The encircling pancreatic tissue surrounds the second part of the duodenum.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain symptoms in annular pancreas?
options: Partial or complete obstruction of the duodenal lumen
Increased bile flow into the intestine
answer: Partial or complete obstruction of the duodenal lumen
explanation: A: Correct. The ring compresses the duodenum from outside. B: Correct. The lumen becomes partially or completely obstructed. C: Correct. Delayed gastric emptying results from duodenal obstruction. D: Incorrect. Bile flow into the intestine is not increased; the obstruction impairs flow. E: Correct. Proximal bowel dilates behind the obstruction.

q: Which of the following are clinical features of annular pancreas?
explanation: A: Correct. Bilious vomiting in neonates indicates obstruction below the ampulla. B: Correct. Feeding intolerance is common. C: Correct. Abdominal distension results from proximal dilation. D: Incorrect. Haematemesis is not a primary feature. E: Correct. Adults may present with recurrent pancreatitis.

q: Which of the following findings support the diagnosis of annular pancreas?
options: CT scan showing pancreatic ring around duodenum
answer: CT scan showing pancreatic ring around duodenum
explanation: A: Correct. The double bubble sign reflects the stomach and proximal duodenum dilated by obstruction. B: Correct. Dilated stomach and proximal duodenum are typical findings. C: Correct. The second part of the duodenum is narrowed by the ring. D: Incorrect. Pancreatic tissue is present in annular pancreas; it surrounds the duodenum. E: Correct. CT can show the pancreatic ring around the duodenum.

q: Which of the following complications can arise from annular pancreas?
explanation: A: Correct. Duodenal obstruction is the main complication. B: Incorrect. Peptic ulcer disease is not a standard complication, and the link is rare and not established in teaching. The key includes this, and I disagree. C: Correct. Recurrent pancreatitis can occur from the ring. D: Incorrect. Biliary obstruction is not a standard complication. Any compression of the bile duct would be rare and not established. The key includes this, and I disagree. E: Incorrect. Appendicitis is not a complication of annular pancreas.

q: Which of the following mechanisms contribute to portal hypertension?
options: Increased resistance to portal blood flow
answer: Increased resistance to portal blood flow
explanation: A: Correct. Increased resistance to portal flow, usually from cirrhosis, raises portal pressure. B: Correct. Increased splanchnic inflow adds to portal pressure. C: Correct. Cirrhotic architectural distortion increases intrahepatic resistance. D: Correct. Portal vein obstruction raises portal pressure. E: Incorrect. Decreased hepatic resistance would lower portal pressure, not raise it.

q: Which of the following sites are common portosystemic anastomoses in portal hypertension?
explanation: A: Correct. Oesophageal submucosal veins form varices. B: Correct. Paraumbilical veins form caput medusae. C: Correct. Rectal veins form haemorrhoids. D: Incorrect. Renal veins are not a portosystemic collateral site. E: Correct. Retroperitoneal veins form collaterals.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain ascites in portal hypertension?
options: Increased hydrostatic pressure in portal circulation
Sodium and water retention via RAAS activation
answer: Increased hydrostatic pressure in portal circulation
Sodium and water retention via RAAS activation
explanation: A: Correct. Raised portal hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid into the peritoneum. B: Correct. Low albumin reduces plasma oncotic pressure. C: Correct. RAAS activation causes sodium and water retention. D: Correct. Lymph production exceeds drainage, and the liver's lymph overflows into the peritoneum. E: Incorrect. Capillary permeability is increased, not decreased, in portal hypertension.

q: Which of the following complications are explained by portal hypertension?
explanation: A: Correct. Raised portal pressure causes oesophageal variceal bleeding. B: Correct. Congestion enlarges the spleen. C: Correct. Hypersplenism causes cytopenias. D: Correct. Portosystemic shunting allows toxins to reach the brain. E: Incorrect. Acute appendicitis is not caused by portal hypertension.

q: Which of the following occur due to portal hypertension?
explanation: A: Correct. Splanchnic vasodilation lowers resistance in the gut. B: Correct. The circulation becomes hyperdynamic. C: Correct. Cardiac output increases. D: Incorrect. Systemic vasodilation, not vasoconstriction, occurs early in portal hypertension. E: Correct. RAAS is activated as effective circulating volume falls.

q: Which of the following explain the pathophysiology of liver injury in trauma?
options: Blunt abdominal trauma causing parenchymal disruption
Rapid deceleration leading to shearing forces
answer: Blunt abdominal trauma causing parenchymal disruption
Rapid deceleration leading to shearing forces
explanation: A: Correct. Blunt force disrupts the parenchyma. B: Correct. Deceleration causes shearing forces across the liver. C: Correct. Lacerations cause the injury. D: Incorrect. The liver does not regenerate fast enough to prevent injury. E: Correct. Injury to hepatic vessels causes bleeding.

q: Which of the following explain bleeding in liver injury?
options: Rich vascular supply (hepatic artery and portal vein)
Immediate clot stabilization in all cases
answer: Rich vascular supply (hepatic artery and portal vein)
explanation: A: Correct. The liver has a rich dual blood supply. B: Correct. The venous system is low-pressure, which affects how bleeding behaves. The key includes this, and it is a reasonable teaching point. C: Correct. Sinusoids are disrupted, causing bleeding. D: Correct. Impaired clotting factor synthesis prolongs bleeding. E: Incorrect. Clot stabilisation is not immediate in all cases; haemorrhage is often ongoing.

q: Which of the following clinical features are explained by liver injury?
options: Referred pain to right shoulder (Kehr’s sign)
answer: Referred pain to right shoulder (Kehr’s sign)
explanation: A: Correct. Liver injury causes right upper quadrant pain. B: Correct. Blood loss causes hypovolaemic shock. C: Correct. Kehr's sign is referred shoulder-tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation. D: Incorrect. Haematuria is not a feature of liver injury. E: Correct. Haemoperitoneum causes distension.

q: Which of the following complications arise due to liver injury?
explanation: A: Correct. Blood collects in the peritoneal cavity. B: Correct. Bile leaks cause a biloma. C: Correct. Infected collections can form abscesses. D: Correct. Coagulopathy follows massive blood loss and transfusion. E: Incorrect. Cirrhosis does not develop immediately after liver injury.

q: Which of the following explain why many liver injuries are managed conservatively?
options: Risk of worsening hemorrhage with unnecessary surgery
answer: Risk of worsening hemorrhage with unnecessary surgery
explanation: A: Correct. The liver regenerates well. B: Correct. Bleeding often tamponades spontaneously. C: Incorrect. Surgery is not always required; many injuries are managed non-operatively. D: Correct. Stable patients can be monitored safely. E: Correct. Unnecessary surgery can worsen haemorrhage and increase complications.

q: Which of the following mechanisms contribute to the formation of a liver abscess?
options: Spread of infection via the portal vein
Ascending infection through the biliary tract
answer: Spread of infection via the portal vein
Ascending infection through the biliary tract
explanation: A: Correct. Infection can spread via the portal vein, for example from the bowel. B: Correct. Infection can ascend through the biliary tract. C: Correct. Bacteraemia can seed the liver through the hepatic artery. D: Correct. Adjacent infection such as from the gallbladder can extend directly into the liver. E: Incorrect. Liver abscesses are infective, not sterile.

q: Which of the following correctly describe types of liver abscess?
options: Amoebic abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica
Viral abscess as a common cause
answer: Amoebic abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica
explanation: A: Correct. Pyogenic abscesses are caused by bacteria. B: Correct. Amoebic abscesses are caused by Entamoeba histolytica. C: Correct. Fungal abscesses occur in immunocompromised patients. D: Incorrect. Viral abscess is not a common cause of liver abscess. E: Correct. Mixed infections occur, especially with polymicrobial sources.

q: Which of the following symptoms/signs are explained by liver abscess?
explanation: A: Correct. Infection causes fever with rigors. B: Correct. The abscess causes right upper quadrant pain. C: Correct. The enlarged liver can be palpated. D: Correct. Jaundice occurs when biliary function is impaired or in severe disease. E: Incorrect. Haematuria is not a feature of liver abscess.

q: Which of the following complications can arise from liver abscess?
explanation: A: Correct. Rupture into the peritoneum causes peritonitis. B: Correct. Rupture into the pleural cavity causes empyema. C: Correct. Bacteraemia causes septicaemia. D: Correct. The abscess can extend upwards into the lung. E: Incorrect. Cirrhosis does not follow immediately from liver abscess.

q: Which of the following are appropriate in evaluating or managing liver abscess?
options: Ultrasound or CT scan for localization
answer: Ultrasound or CT scan for localization
explanation: A: Correct. Ultrasound or CT localises the abscess. B: Correct. Aspiration confirms the diagnosis and drains the abscess. C: Correct. Antibiotics treat the infection. D: Incorrect. Liver transplantation is not an immediate treatment for abscess. E: Correct. Serology confirms amoebic abscess.

q: Which of the following mechanisms contribute to the development of ascites?
options: Increased hydrostatic pressure in portal circulation
Activation of RAAS leading to sodium retention
answer: Increased hydrostatic pressure in portal circulation
Activation of RAAS leading to sodium retention
explanation: A: Correct. Raised portal pressure drives fluid into the peritoneum. B: Correct. Low albumin reduces oncotic pressure. C: Correct. RAAS activation drives sodium retention. D: Correct. Increased sinusoidal and capillary permeability contributes to fluid leak. This is accepted in teaching, though less central than the first three. E: Incorrect. Lymph production increases in ascites, rather than decreases.

q: Which of the following explain ascites specifically in cirrhosis?
explanation: A: Correct. Increased intrahepatic resistance raises portal pressure. B: Correct. Splanchnic vasodilation lowers effective arterial volume. C: Correct. Effective arterial underfilling drives sodium retention. D: Correct. Renal sodium retention maintains the fluid build-up. E: Incorrect. Systemic vascular resistance falls in cirrhosis, not rises.

q: Which of the following are clinical features of ascites?
explanation: A: Correct. Fluid causes abdominal distension. B: Correct. Shifting dullness is elicited by percussion as fluid moves. C: Correct. A fluid thrill can be felt across the abdomen. D: Correct. Fluid retention causes peripheral oedema. E: Incorrect. Bowel sounds are typically reduced, not hyperactive, in ascites.

q: Which of the following complications arise from ascites?
explanation: A: Correct. Infected ascitic fluid causes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. B: Correct. Hepatorenal syndrome occurs in advanced ascites. C: Correct. Large ascites impairs diaphragmatic movement and breathing. D: Correct. Ascites raises intra-abdominal pressure, promoting umbilical hernia. E: Incorrect. Acute pancreatitis is not caused by ascites.

q: Which of the following are important in evaluating ascites?
explanation: A: Correct. SAAG separates portal hypertensive from other causes. B: Correct. Cell count detects infection such as SBP. C: Correct. Fluid culture identifies the organism. D: Incorrect. Serum amylase is not needed for all cases of ascites. E: Correct. Ultrasound confirms and guides sampling.

q: Which of the following describe the pathophysiology of papillary thyroid carcinoma?
explanation: A: Correct. PTC arises from follicular epithelial cells. B: Correct. BRAF V600E mutation is the most common driver. C: Correct. Radiation exposure is a recognised risk factor. D: Incorrect. PTC does not produce calcitonin; that is a feature of MTC. E: Correct. Papillary architecture is the defining histological pattern.

q: Which of the following explain the spread of papillary thyroid carcinoma?
options: Lymphatic spread to cervical lymph nodes
Direct spread to spleen is common
answer: Lymphatic spread to cervical lymph nodes
explanation: A: Correct. PTC spreads early via lymphatics to cervical nodes. B: Incorrect. Haematogenous spread is late, not early, in PTC. C: Correct. Regional lymph nodes are commonly involved. D: Correct. Skip metastasis to distant nodes can occur. E: Incorrect. The spleen is not a common site of direct spread.

q: Which of the following are characteristic histological features of papillary carcinoma?
explanation: A: Correct. Orphan Annie eye nuclei are a classic feature of PTC. B: Correct. Psammoma bodies are typical. C: Correct. Nuclear grooves are characteristic. D: Incorrect. Follicular invasion is a feature of follicular carcinoma, not classic PTC. E: Correct. Ground-glass (optically clear) nuclei are a classic finding.

q: Which of the following are typical clinical features of papillary thyroid carcinoma?
options: Hoarseness due to recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement
answer: Hoarseness due to recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement
explanation: A: Correct. A painless nodule is the typical presentation. B: Correct. Cervical lymphadenopathy is common. C: Incorrect. PTC causes slow, painless enlargement, not rapid severe pain. D: Correct. Most patients are euthyroid. E: Correct. Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement causes hoarseness.

q: Which of the following are appropriate management strategies for papillary thyroid carcinoma?
explanation: A: Correct. Total thyroidectomy is standard for most PTC. B: Correct. RAI is used for ablation in higher-risk patients. C: Correct. TSH suppression reduces recurrence in differentiated thyroid cancer. D: Correct. Thyroglobulin monitors for recurrence. E: Incorrect. Chemotherapy is not first-line; PTC is usually treated surgically.

q: Which of the following mechanisms contribute to the development of goiter?
options: Increased thyroid hormone levels suppressing TSH
explanation: A: Correct. Chronic TSH stimulation drives gland growth. B: Correct. Iodine deficiency reduces hormone synthesis and raises TSH. C: Correct. Impaired hormone synthesis raises TSH and enlarges the gland. D: Incorrect. Raised thyroid hormone suppresses TSH and does not cause goitre. E: Correct. Follicular hyperplasia enlarges the gland.

q: Which of the following correctly describe types of goiter?
options: Diffuse goiter due to uniform gland enlargement
Multinodular goiter due to repeated cycles of stimulation
Endemic goiter linked to iodine deficiency
answer: Diffuse goiter due to uniform gland enlargement
Multinodular goiter due to repeated cycles of stimulation
Endemic goiter linked to iodine deficiency
explanation: A: Correct. Diffuse goitre enlarges the gland uniformly. B: Correct. Multinodular goitre develops from repeated cycles of stimulation and repair. C: Correct. Toxic goitre is associated with hyperthyroidism. D: Incorrect. Simple goitre is euthyroid and does not always cause hyperthyroidism. E: Correct. Endemic goitre is caused by iodine deficiency.

q: Which of the following features are due to enlargement of the thyroid gland?
explanation: A: Correct. Neck swelling is the direct effect of enlargement. B: Correct. Enlargement can compress the oesophagus, causing dysphagia. C: Correct. Enlargement compresses the trachea, causing dyspnoea. D: Correct. Enlargement can compress the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness. E: Incorrect. Haematuria is not caused by thyroid enlargement.

q: Which of the following explain hyperthyroidism in toxic goiter?
explanation: A: Correct. Autonomous hormone production causes the thyrotoxicosis. B: Correct. Activity is TSH-independent. C: Incorrect. Toxic goitre is autonomous, not increased sensitivity to TSH. D: Correct. Circulating T3 and T4 are raised. E: Correct. TSH is suppressed by the excess hormone.

q: Which of the following complications can arise from long-standing goiter?
explanation: A: Correct. Enlargement can compress the trachea. B: Correct. Goitre can extend retrosternally, causing compression. C: Correct. Retrosternal goitre can obstruct the superior vena cava. D: Correct. Long-standing goitre carries a risk of malignant change. E: Incorrect. Acute appendicitis is not a complication of goitre.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain thyroiditis?
options: Increased synthesis of new thyroid hormones
Transient hyperthyroid phase followed by hypothyroidism
answer: Transient hyperthyroid phase followed by hypothyroidism
explanation: A: Correct. Thyroiditis is inflammation of thyroid tissue. B: Correct. Preformed hormone is released from damaged follicles. C: Correct. Autoimmune destruction is a common mechanism. D: Incorrect. New hormone synthesis is typically reduced in thyroiditis, not increased. E: Correct. Many thyroiditides show a transient hyperthyroid phase followed by hypothyroidism.

q: Which of the following are features of subacute thyroiditis?
explanation: A: Correct. The gland is painful and tender. B: Correct. The cause is thought to be viral. C: Correct. ESR is markedly raised. D: Incorrect. Radioactive iodine uptake is low, not increased, because the release is of preformed hormone. E: Correct. Transient hyperthyroidism occurs.

q: Which of the following explain Hashimoto thyroiditis?
explanation: A: Correct. Autoimmune destruction of follicles is the mechanism. B: Correct. Anti-TPO antibodies are typical. C: Correct. Lymphocytic infiltration is the histological hallmark. D: Correct. Progressive hypothyroidism results from follicle loss. E: Incorrect. RAI uptake is typically low or normal in Hashimoto thyroiditis, not increased.

q: Which of the following describe postpartum thyroiditis?
explanation: A: Correct. It occurs after pregnancy. B: Correct. It has an autoimmune mechanism. C: Correct. A transient hyperthyroid phase is typical. D: Correct. A hypothyroid phase often follows. E: Incorrect. Postpartum thyroiditis is managed medically; surgery is not required.

q: Which of the following help distinguish thyroiditis from Graves’ disease?
explanation: A: Correct. RAI uptake is low in thyroiditis, unlike Graves'. B: Correct. Graves' disease has TSH receptor antibodies, which thyroiditis does not. C: Correct. Pain is a feature of subacute thyroiditis. D: Incorrect. Hormone synthesis is increased in Graves' disease, not in thyroiditis. E: Correct. Thyroiditis is typically transient, while Graves' is persistent.

q: Which of the following mechanisms are central to the development of acute pancreatitis?
options: Premature activation of trypsin within pancreatic acinar cells
Gallstone obstruction at the ampulla of Vater
answer: Premature activation of trypsin within pancreatic acinar cells
Gallstone obstruction at the ampulla of Vater
explanation: A: Correct. Premature trypsin activation starts the cascade. B: Correct. Autodigestion damages the pancreas. C: Correct. Gallstone obstruction at the ampulla is a major cause. D: Correct. Alcohol injures acinar cells and is a major cause. E: Not applicable. Option E is not listed in this question.

q: Which of the following explain the characteristic pain in pancreatitis?
options: Radiation of pain to the back
answer: Radiation of pain to the back
explanation: A: Correct. Inflammation of the pancreas causes the pain. B: Correct. Retroperitoneal irritation contributes to the pain. C: Correct. Pain radiates to the back. D: Incorrect. Pain is relieved by sitting forward, not by lying flat. E: Correct. Pain is typically worsened after meals.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain systemic complications in pancreatitis?
explanation: A: Correct. Cytokines drive the systemic response. B: Correct. Vascular permeability increases, causing fluid leak. C: Correct. Third spacing of fluid occurs. D: Correct. Hypovolaemic shock can follow fluid loss. E: Arguable. Immunosuppression (the late compensatory phase) is recognised in severe disease, but it is not standard teaching for early systemic complications. The key excludes this, and I agree with the key.

q: Which of the following mechanisms explain complications of acute pancreatitis?
options: Fat necrosis due to lipase activity
answer: Fat necrosis due to lipase activity
explanation: A: Correct. Lipase causes fat necrosis. B: Correct. Calcium binds fatty acids in saponification, causing hypocalcaemia. C: Correct. Fluid collections form pseudocysts. D: Correct. Vessel erosion causes haemorrhage. E: Incorrect. Fibrosis develops in chronic disease, not early in acute pancreatitis.

q: Which of the following findings are explained by the pathophysiology of pancreatitis?
options: Hyperglycemia due to islet cell injury
answer: Hyperglycemia due to islet cell injury
explanation: A: Correct. Pancreatic injury raises amylase and lipase. B: Correct. Ileus reduces bowel sounds. C: Correct. Islet cell injury causes hyperglycaemia. D: Correct. Inflammation causes fever. E: Incorrect. Calcium is typically low, not raised, in pancreatitis.

q: Which of the following are essential components of a complete surgical history?
explanation: A: Correct. The presenting complaint is a core component. B: Correct. The history of the presenting illness is a core component. C: Correct. The past surgical history is a core component. D: Correct. The family history is part of a complete history. E: Correct. The social history is part of a complete history.

q: Which of the following should be included when exploring the history of presenting illness?
explanation: A: Correct. Onset is essential to the history. B: Correct. Duration and progression are essential. C: Correct. Associated symptoms help the differential. D: Incorrect. Occupation belongs to the social history, not the presenting illness. E: Correct. Aggravating and relieving factors are essential.

q: Which of the following are important when taking past surgical history?
explanation: A: Correct. Previous operations must be recorded. B: Correct. The indication for each operation is important. C: Correct. Complications of previous surgery are important. D: Correct. The type of anaesthesia can reveal problems such as difficult airway or malignant hyperthermia. E: Incorrect. Food preferences are not relevant to surgical history.

q: Which of the following are important in surgical drug history?
explanation: A: Correct. Current medications must be recorded. B: Correct. Anticoagulants affect bleeding risk. C: Correct. Drug allergies are essential for safe prescribing. D: Correct. Herbal medicines can interact with anaesthesia and surgery. E: Incorrect. Blood group is not part of the drug history.

q: Which aspects of social history are important in surgical patients?
explanation: A: Correct. Smoking affects wound healing and surgical risk. B: Correct. Alcohol affects anaesthesia, healing and withdrawal risk. C: Correct. Occupation can influence fitness, exposure and recovery. D: Correct. Living conditions affect discharge planning. E: Incorrect. Eye colour is not relevant to surgical history.

q: Which of the following are considered red flag symptoms in surgical patients?
explanation: A: Correct. Unintentional weight loss suggests malignancy. B: Correct. Persistent vomiting suggests obstruction or other serious pathology. C: Correct. Severe abdominal pain can indicate a surgical emergency. D: Correct. Night sweats can indicate malignancy or infection. E: Incorrect. Mild headache is not a surgical red flag in this context.

q: Which of the following contribute to the development of hepatocellular carcinoma?
explanation: A: Correct. Chronic hepatitis B is a major risk factor. B: Correct. Chronic hepatitis C is a major risk factor. C: Correct. Cirrhosis from any cause raises HCC risk. D: Correct. Aflatoxin exposure is a recognised risk factor. E: Incorrect. Acute appendicitis is not a risk factor for HCC.

q: Which of the following explain the mechanism of hepatocellular carcinoma?
options: Chronic inflammation leading to hepatocyte injury
Repeated cycles of regeneration and mutation
answer: Chronic inflammation leading to hepatocyte injury
Repeated cycles of regeneration and mutation
explanation: A: Correct. Chronic inflammation drives carcinogenesis. B: Correct. Repeated regeneration increases the chance of mutation. C: Correct. TP53 mutations such as p53 are involved. D: Incorrect. Apoptosis is reduced in HCC, which allows tumour growth. E: Correct. Dysplastic nodules are precursors of HCC.

q: Which of the following are typical features of hepatocellular carcinoma?
explanation: A: Correct. Right upper quadrant pain is common. B: Correct. Weight loss is a frequent feature. C: Correct. Hepatomegaly is common. D: Correct. Jaundice occurs with advanced disease. E: Incorrect. Haematuria is not a feature of HCC.

q: Which of the following are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma?
explanation: A: Correct. Alpha-fetoprotein is a tumour marker raised in HCC. B: Correct. Hypoglycaemia can be paraneoplastic. C: Correct. Erythropoietin production can cause polycythaemia. D: Correct. Ectopic PTH-related peptide can cause hypercalcaemia. E: Incorrect. TSH is not raised by HCC.

q: Which of the following complications are explained by hepatocellular carcinoma?
explanation: A: Correct. The tumour can invade the portal vein. B: Correct. Portal vein invasion and cirrhosis cause portal hypertension. C: Correct. Portal hypertension leads to ascites. D: Correct. HCC metastasises to the lungs. E: Incorrect. HCC does not cause acute pancreatitis.

q: Which of the following mechanisms can lead to an acute abdomen?
explanation: A: Correct. Inflammation such as appendicitis causes acute abdomen. B: Correct. Perforation of a hollow organ causes peritonitis. C: Correct. Bowel obstruction causes acute abdomen. D: Correct. Ischaemia causes acute abdomen. E: Incorrect. A chronic stable condition is not an acute abdomen.

q: Which of the following are common causes of acute abdomen?
explanation: A: Correct. Appendicitis is the commonest cause. B: Correct. Acute cholecystitis is a common cause. C: Correct. Acute pancreatitis is a common cause. D: Correct. Perforated peptic ulcer causes acute abdomen. E: Incorrect. Controlled hypertension is not a cause of acute abdomen.

q: Which of the following signs indicate peritoneal irritation?
explanation: A: Correct. Rebound tenderness indicates peritoneal irritation. B: Correct. Guarding is a protective reflex from peritoneal irritation. C: Correct. Board-like rigidity indicates peritonitis. D: Incorrect. Increased bowel sounds suggest obstruction, not peritonism. E: Correct. Reduced bowel sounds from ileus occur in peritonitis.

q: Which of the following systemic features may occur in acute abdomen?
explanation: A: Correct. Fever reflects the inflammatory response. B: Correct. Tachycardia reflects the systemic response. C: Correct. Hypotension occurs in severe or late disease. D: Correct. Leucocytosis reflects the inflammatory response. E: Incorrect. Bradycardia is not a typical feature.

q: Which of the following indicate a surgical emergency in acute abdomen?
explanation: A: Correct. Signs of peritonitis mandate surgery. B: Correct. Haemodynamic instability indicates a surgical emergency. C: Correct. Persistent vomiting with obstruction requires urgent surgery. D: Correct. Sudden severe pain suggests perforation. E: Incorrect. Mild intermittent discomfort is not a surgical emergency.

q: Which of the following mechanisms contribute to the formation of an appendiceal abscess?
options: Localized containment of infection by omentum
Spread of infection throughout the entire peritoneal cavity immediately
Formation of a localized pus collection
Immune response limiting spread of infection
answer: Localized containment of infection by omentum
Formation of a localized pus collection
Immune response limiting spread of infection
explanation: A: Correct. Perforation of the appendix releases infection locally. B: Correct. The omentum contains the infection. C: Incorrect. Infection is contained, not spread immediately throughout the peritoneum. D: Correct. A localised pus collection forms the abscess. E: Correct. The immune response limits spread.

q: Which of the following are typical features of appendiceal abscess?
options: Palpable tender mass in right iliac fossa
answer: Palpable tender mass in right iliac fossa
explanation: A: Correct. Pain persists in the right lower quadrant. B: Correct. Fever is typical. C: Correct. A tender mass is palpable in the right iliac fossa. D: Incorrect. Sudden complete relief of pain suggests perforation, not abscess. E: Correct. Leucocytosis is typical.

q: Which of the following are appropriate management strategies for appendiceal abscess?
explanation: A: Correct. IV antibiotics treat the infection. B: Correct. Image-guided drainage is used for larger abscesses. C: Incorrect. Immediate surgery is not needed in all cases. D: Correct. Interval appendicectomy follows resolution. E: Incorrect. Observation alone without treatment is unsafe.

q: Which of the following mechanisms contribute to large bowel obstruction?
explanation: A: Correct. Mechanical blockage causes obstruction. B: Correct. Colonic distension progresses behind the obstruction. C: Correct. Intraluminal pressure rises. D: Incorrect. Bacterial activity increases gas production; decreased activity is not a mechanism. E: Correct. Raised pressure risks bowel wall ischaemia.

q: Which of the following are common causes of LBO?
explanation: A: Correct. Colorectal carcinoma is the commonest cause of LBO in adults. B: Correct. Sigmoid volvulus causes LBO. C: Correct. Faecal impaction causes LBO. D: Incorrect. Adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction, not large bowel obstruction. E: Correct. Diverticular stricture causes LBO.

q: Which of the following are typical features of large bowel obstruction?
explanation: A: Correct. Distension develops as gas and fluid accumulate. B: Correct. Constipation or obstipation occurs. C: Correct. Vomiting is a late feature in LBO. D: Correct. Colicky pain occurs as peristalsis works against the obstruction. E: Incorrect. Early profuse vomiting is typical of small bowel obstruction, not large bowel.

q: Which of the following complications can arise from untreated large bowel obstruction?
explanation: A: Correct. Ischaemia can follow raised pressure. B: Correct. The caecum is at risk of perforation. C: Correct. Perforation causes peritonitis. D: Correct. Infection leads to sepsis. E: Incorrect. Pancreatitis is not a direct complication of LBO.

q: Which of the following explain closed-loop obstruction in large bowel?
explanation: A: Correct. The loop is obstructed at two points. B: Correct. A competent ileocaecal valve traps the loop. C: Correct. Pressure rises rapidly within the closed loop. D: Incorrect. A closed loop does not decompress into the small bowel. E: Correct. The high pressure increases the risk of perforation.

q: Which of the following are appropriate in managing large bowel obstruction?
explanation: A: Correct. Fluid resuscitation is essential. B: Correct. Nasogastric decompression reduces vomiting and distension. C: Correct. Complete obstruction needs surgical management. D: Correct. Colonoscopic decompression can untwist a sigmoid volvulus. E: Incorrect. Immediate discharge is unsafe in LBO.

q: Which of the following mechanisms lead to the formation of an appendicular abscess?
options: Immediate spread of infection to entire peritoneal cavity
Fibrin deposition forming a localized wall
answer: Fibrin deposition forming a localized wall
explanation: A: Correct. Perforation of an inflamed appendix starts the abscess. B: Correct. The omentum contains the infection, known as the abdominal policeman. C: Incorrect. Infection is contained and does not spread immediately across the peritoneum. D: Correct. Fibrin forms a localised wall around the collection. E: Correct. Adjacent bowel loops adhere to wall off the infection.

q: Which of the following are typical features of appendicular abscess?
options: Palpable tender mass in right lower abdomen
answer: Palpable tender mass in right lower abdomen
explanation: A: Correct. Right iliac fossa pain persists. B: Correct. Fever with chills is typical. C: Correct. A tender mass is palpable. D: Incorrect. Sudden disappearance of pain suggests perforation, not abscess. E: Correct. Leucocytosis is typical.

q: Which of the following explain why the infection remains localized in appendicular abscess?
explanation: A: Correct. The omentum wraps around the appendix to contain infection. B: Correct. The local immune response contains infection. C: Correct. Adhesions form between tissues to wall off infection. D: Incorrect. Raised intra-abdominal pressure would spread infection, not localise it. E: Correct. Fibrin deposition creates a barrier.

q: Which of the following complications may occur?
explanation: A: Correct. Rupture of the abscess causes generalised peritonitis. B: Correct. Sepsis can follow abscess rupture or spread. C: Correct. Adhesions can cause intestinal obstruction. D: Correct. Fistulae can form, especially with bowel. E: Incorrect. Myocardial infarction is not a complication of appendicular abscess.

q: Which of the following are appropriate management strategies?
explanation: A: Correct. IV antibiotics treat the infection. B: Correct. Image-guided drainage treats larger collections. C: Incorrect. Immediate appendicectomy in all patients is not appropriate; abscess is managed first. D: Correct. Interval appendicectomy follows resolution. E: Incorrect. Observation alone without treatment is unsafe.
